title: From Sensory Schema to Boolean Algebra: A Sensory-Motivated Interpretation of Classical Logic
content: While Boolean algebra is conventionally formalised as an axiomatic system, this paper develops a sensory-motivated interpretation of it, grounded in an informal model of sensory experience: the sensory schema. More broadly, the paper contributes to the philosophy of logic and mathematics by offering an account of the cognitive origin of Boolean structure, locating it within an independently motivated model of embodied sensory cognition rather than treating it as a mind-independent given. The schema describes experience as the product of two orthogonal aspects: an intensive aspect (private, qualitative, inexpressible) and an extensive aspect (private, spatial, measurable, yet publicly expressible). When the intensive aspect of the product is bracketed, the remaining public domain consists of a complete tiling of locations, each either occupied by a column of discrete units or bare. Three operations defined on this domain (pattern-union, pattern-overlap, pattern-inversion) coincide exactly with Boolean union, intersection, and complement, and each Boolean law holds as a direct structural fact about tile occupancy. The post-reduction domain is isomorphic to the Boolean algebra P(T), the power set of the set of tiles T, with the isomorphism mediated by spatial structure alone rather than prior logical axioms. The paper’s contribution is this precise, non-metaphorical correspondence between a specific experiential reduction and a specific formal system; Section 4 extends the picture, showing the same public domain also supports fuzzy sets and multisets under different selections, situating Boolean algebra as one motivated projection among several rather than a unique terminus. Read against embodied-cognition accounts of mathematics, which explain where mathematical ideas come from but not why their laws must hold, this bracketing-and-verification strategy makes a stronger claim: embodied cognition can ground logical necessity itself, not only its psychological origin.
